title: Linked List Cycle II
statement:
`head` is the first node of a singly linked list, or `null` when the list is empty. Following `next` pointers from `head` may eventually bring you back to a node you already passed, which means the list contains a loop. Return the node where that loop begins, which is the first node reached a second time, or `null` when following `next` ends at `null`. Leave the list unchanged.

Each case is written as `[head, pos]`: the node values in order, and `pos`, the 0-based index of the node that the last node's `next` points to (`-1` means it points to `null`). Your function receives only the head node and never sees `pos`. The result is shown as the index of the node you return, or `-1` for `null`.
constraints: The list has between 0 and 10^4 nodes
pos is -1 or the index of a node in the list
notes:
## Intuition

Remembering every visited node in a set finds the answer directly: the first node met twice is where the loop starts. That needs O(n) extra memory. Floyd's fast and slow pointers need O(1): `fast` moves two nodes per round and `slow` one. Without a loop, `fast` runs off the end. With one, both end up circling it and `fast` gains one node per round, so they must meet.

Why the meeting point helps: let `a` be the steps from the head to the loop start, `c` the loop length, and say they meet `b` steps into the loop. `slow` walked `a + b` steps and `fast` twice that, so the extra `a + b` is a whole number of laps `k·c`. Hence `a = k·c - b`: walking `a` steps from the meeting point lands on the loop start, exactly where a pointer walking `a` steps from the head arrives.

## Approach

1. Start `slow` and `fast` at `head`.
2. While `fast` and `fast.next` exist, move `slow` one node and `fast` two.
3. If they land on the same node, there is a loop: start `entry` at `head`.
4. Move `entry` and `slow` one node at a time until they are the same node, and return it.
5. If `fast` reaches the end, return `null`.

## Example 1, step by step

The list is `3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4`, and `-4` links back to index 1.

- Round 1: `slow` at index 1, `fast` at index 2.
- Round 2: `slow` at index 2, `fast` at index 1 (3, then back to 1).
- Round 3: `slow` at index 3, `fast` at index 3: they meet.
- `entry` starts at index 0. One step moves `entry` to index 1 and `slow` from index 3 to index 1. They are the same node, so index 1 is returned.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): `slow` takes at most about n steps before the meeting, and the second phase at most n more.
- Space: O(1): three pointers.

## Pitfalls

- Check `fast !== null && fast.next !== null` before jumping two nodes, or lists without a loop crash.
- Compare nodes, not values: values repeat, as in `[7,7,7,7]`.
- Start both pointers at `head`; starting `fast` one node ahead shifts the meeting point and the second phase misses the start.
- Do not mark nodes by changing `val` or `next`; the list must stay as it was.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `slow` | pointer that moves one node per round |
| `fast` | pointer that moves two nodes per round |
| `entry` | pointer that walks from the head to the loop start |

narration.2: slow will move one node per round.
narration.3: fast starts at the same node and will move two nodes per round.
narration.4: Keep going while fast can jump two nodes; if it cannot, the list ends and has no loop.
narration.7: The pointers can only land on the same node inside a loop.
narration.8: A new pointer starts back at the head.
narration.9: Walk entry and slow together until they meet.
narration.10: entry moves one node toward the loop start from the head...
narration.11: ...while slow moves the same distance on from the meeting point.
narration.13: They meet exactly at the first node of the loop.
narration.16: fast ran off the end of the list, so there is no loop.
